This property describes the version of the place the server is running on.

This version number corresponds with the version number shown under the Version History section of the place's settings. It is not the current version of the Roblox client. This property is 0 for all unpublished experiences.

When a server instance is created for a place, it uses the place's current version. If the place is later updated while this server is running, the server will remain at its current version.

m.d:
This property describes the private server ID of the server, if the server is a private server.

If the server is not a private server, then this property will be an empty string.

Private servers

Private servers refer to the following:

  • Private servers that users can purchase from the games page
  • Reserved servers, private servers created by the developer using TeleportService:ReserveServerAsync()

PrivateServerId vs JobId

The PrivateServerId of a server is different from the DataModel.JobId. The JobId is the unique identifier of the current server instance.

Private servers (private or reserved servers) can have multiple server instances associated with them over time. This is because, although only one server instance can be running at once for a private server, new server instances can open and close as players join and leave the game. For example, no server instance is running when nobody is playing in the server. The PrivateServerId will be consistent across all of these server instances, and the DataModel.JobId will be unique for each one.

See also:

  • DataModel.PrivateServerOwnerId, a property describing the owner of a private server
  • TeleportService:ReserveServerAsync(), a function which creates a reserved server
m.s: Describes the private server ID of the server, if the server is a private server or a `Class.TeleportService:ReserveServerAsync()|reserved server`.

m.d:
This property describes the UserId of the Player that owns the private server if the server is private.

If the server is a standard or reserved server then this property will be set to 0.

This property could be used to identify if a Player is the owner of the private server, for example:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

-- is this a private server?
if game.PrivateServerId ~= "" and game.PrivateServerOwnerId ~= 0 then

    -- listen for new players being added
    Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)

        -- check if the player is the server owner
        if player.UserId == game.PrivateServerOwnerId then
            print("The private server owner has joined the game")
        end
    end)
end

See also:

  • DataModel.PrivateServerId, a property describing the unique ID of private and reserved servers
m.s: Describes the `Class.Player.UserId|UserId` of the `Class.Player` that owns the private server if the server is private.

m.d:
Binds a function to be called before the server shuts down. If the bound function accepts a parameter, it passes CloseReason specifying the reason for the server shutdown.

You can bind multiple functions by calling BindToClose() repeatedly. Bound functions are called in parallel and run at the same time.

The experience server waits 30 seconds for all bound functions to stop running before it shuts down. After 30 seconds, the server shuts down even if functions are still running. Teleports are disabled during moderation shutdowns.

To verify that the current session is not in Roblox Studio, use RunService:IsStudio(). This prevents bound functions from completing their run in offline testing sessions.

When you use DataStoreService, you should also use BindToClose to bind a function saving all unsaved data to DataStores. This prevents data loss if the server shuts down unexpectedly.

See also:

  • CloseReason for reasons for the experience server shutdown.
  • PluginGui:BindToClose(), which binds a function to a PluginGui close button.
m.s: Binds a function to be called before the server shuts down.

p.s: A function called before the experience server shuts down. If the bound function accepts a parameter, it passes CloseReason specifying the reason for the server shutdown.

m.d:
Returns a table containing basic information about the jobs performed by the task scheduler.

In computing, a task scheduler is a system responsible for executing key tasks at the appropriate intervals.

You can also find live task scheduler statistics in the Task Scheduler window in Roblox Studio.

The first entry in the table returned is a reference dictionary containing the statistics (or headings) available. It is in the following format:

{
    ["name"] = "name",
    ["averageDutyCycle"] = "averageDutyCycle",
    ["averageStepsPerSecond"] = "averageStepsPerSecond",
    ["averageStepTime"] = "averageStepTime",
    ["averageError"] = "averageError",
    ["isRunning"] = "isRunning",
}

The subsequent entries in the table returned are dictionaries containing the above statistics for jobs performed by the task scheduler. For example:

{
    ["name"] = "Heartbeat",
    ["averageDutyCycle"] = 0,
    ["averageStepsPerSecond"] = 0,
    ["averageStepTime"] = 0,
    ["averageError"] = 0,
    ["isRunning"] = false,
}

See also:

  • TaskScheduler
m.s: Returns a table containing basic information about the jobs performed by the task scheduler.

r.s: A table containing information about the jobs performed by the task scheduler, see above for the format.

Fires when the user prompts an increase or decrease in graphics quality using the hotkeys.

This event fires under the following conditions:

  • If the user presses F10, this event fires with a betterQuality argument of true.
  • If the user presses ShiftF10, this event fires with a betterQuality argument of false.

This event does not provide the current graphics quality level or cover all updates to the graphics quality. For example, changes made in the core GUI escape menu are not registered.

You can retrieve a user's SavedQualitySetting using UserGameSettings with the following snippet:

UserSettings():GetService("UserGameSettings").SavedQualityLevel

If the user's graphics settings are set to automatic then the SavedQualitySetting will be Automatic. There is currently no way for developers to reliably get the current graphics quality level of a user's machine.
m.s: Fires when the user prompts and increase or decrease in graphics quality using the hotkeys.

p.s: Whether the user has prompted an increase (true) or a decrease (false) in graphics quality.

Fires when the server has been scheduled to restart, for example when you restart servers from the Creator Hub or Open Cloud to release an experience update, or when Roblox needs to restart servers for infrastructure maintenance.

You can use this event to inform players on the server of the impending restart. You could then let them save their progress or teleport them to updated servers at the most convenient time for your game.
m.s: Fires on the server when the server has been scheduled to restart. Provides the scheduled restart time, source, and custom attributes.

p.s: A DateTime indicating when the server is scheduled to shut down. The actual restart may happen slightly after this projected time, but not before.
An CloseReason describing what triggered the restart. The value will be CloseReason.DeveloperUpdate for experience updates, and CloseReason.RobloxMaintenance for server maintenance updates.
A dictionary of developer-supplied metadata associated with the restart. If no attributes are provided, then this will be an empty table.

class/DataModelMesh.d:
The DataModelMesh is an abstract class from which mesh classes descend.

Mesh classes are objects that, when parented to BaseParts alter the appearance of the part to that of a predefined mesh. Note, they only alter the appearance of the part and not the physics/collision boundaries of the part. Developers looking to apply a mesh to a part that alters the part's collision should use MeshParts.

Note the MeshPart and CharacterMesh classes do not descend from DataModelMesh.
class/DataModelMesh.s: The DataModelMesh is an abstract class from which mesh classes descend.

m.d:
The Offset of a mesh determines the distance from the BasePart.Position of a BasePart that the mesh will be displayed.

How to use mesh offset

The Offset property changes the relative position the mesh will be rendered at. For example, an offset of 0, 5, 0 will cause the mesh to be displayed 5 studs above the position of the BasePart.

The position of the BasePart remains unchanged, meaning the physics collision box of the part will remain in the same location. This is demonstrated in the image below where the green outline (a SelectionBox) shows the extents of the BasePart.

Other uses for mesh offset

There are a number of interesting uses for the mesh offset property.

  • Offset and DataModelMesh.Scale can be animated using TweenService relatively inexpensively as the engine does not need to make any physics/collision calculations as the BasePart is not moved.
  • Changing the relationship between the mesh and its collision extents (determined by the BasePart)
m.s: The Offset of a mesh determines the relative position from the `Class.BasePart.Position` of a `Class.BasePart` that the mesh will be displayed at.

m.d:
The Scale of a mesh determines the size of the mesh relative to its original dimensions.

How to use mesh scale

The scale property works slightly differently depending on the type of mesh being used. Note the size of the BasePart remains unchanged, meaning the physics collision box of the part will remain the same.

  • SpecialMesh objects with SpecialMesh.FileType set to 'FileMesh' scale relative to the original dimensions of the mesh when it was uploaded to Roblox
  • BlockMesh objects or SpecialMesh objects with SpecialMesh.FileType set to 'Brick', 'Wedge' or 'Sphere' scale uniformly relative to the BasePart.Size of their parent
  • CylinderMesh objects or SpecialMesh objects with SpecialMesh.FileType set to 'Cylinder' scale relative to the BasePart.Size of their parent. Uniformly for the cylinders height axis and maintaining a 1:1 ratio for the length and width of the cylinder, using the lowest value.
  • SpecialMesh objects with SpecialMesh.FileType set to 'Head' currently scale in a non standard manner. Developers should not rely on this as there are plans to change this behavior.
  • SpecialMesh objects with SpecialMesh.FileType set to 'Torso' scale in a non standard manner. Developers should not rely on this as there are plans to deprecate this mesh type.

Mesh scale demonstration

The above behavior can be seen in the following demonstration images.

Linear scaling relative to part size for 'Brick', 'Wedge' and 'Sphere' meshes.

Linear scaling relative to original uploaded mesh for 'FileMesh' meshes

Non-uniform constrained scaling for 'Cylinder' meshes

Other uses for mesh scale

There are a number of interesting uses for the mesh offset property.

  • DataModelMesh.Offset and Scale can be animated using TweenService relatively inexpensively as the engine does not need to make any physics/collision calculations as the BasePart is not changed.
  • Changing the relationship between the mesh and its collision extents (determined by the BasePart)
m.s: The Scale of a mesh determines the size of the mesh relative to its original dimensions.

class/DataStore.d: See Data stores for an in-depth guide on data structure, management, error handling, limits, and more.
class/DataStore.s: A `Class.GlobalDataStore` that also supports versioning, key metadata, and enumerating keys.

m.d: This function retrieves the specified key version as well as a DataStoreKeyInfo instance. A version identifier can be found through DataStore:ListVersionsAsync() or alternatively be the identifier returned by GlobalDataStore:SetAsync().
m.s: Retrieves the specified key version.

p.s: Key name for which the version info is requested. If DataStoreOptions.AllScopes was set to true when accessing the data store through DataStoreService:GetDataStore(), this key name must be prepended with the original scope as in "scope/key".
Version number of the key for which the version info is requested.

r.s: The value of the key at the specified version and a DataStoreKeyInfo instance that includes the version number, date and time the version was created, and functions to retrieve UserIds and metadata.

kid.simple: Reads one specific older version of a key. The version id comes from `ListVersionsAsync` or from the return value of `SetAsync`.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")

local ok, versionId = pcall(function()
	return store:SetAsync("User_1", { Coins = 5 }) -- returns the new version id
end)
if ok then
	local ok2, value = pcall(function()
		return store:GetVersionAsync("User_1", versionId)
	end)
	print(ok2, value)
end

m.d: This function retrieves the key version that was current at a given time as well as a DataStoreKeyInfo instance.
m.s: Retrieves the key version that was current at a given time.

p.s: Key name for which the version info is requested. If DataStoreOptions.AllScopes was set to true when accessing the data store through DataStoreService:GetDataStore(), this key name must be prepended with the original scope as in "scope/key".
Unix timestamp in milliseconds for which the requested version was current. Must be greater than zero. Must not be more than ten minutes in the future.

r.s: The value of the key that was current at the specified time and a DataStoreKeyInfo instance that includes the version number, date and time the version was created, and functions to retrieve UserIds and metadata. nil if no available version was current at the requested time.

kid.simple: Reads whatever value a key had at a certain moment. You give the time as a Unix timestamp in milliseconds.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")

local yesterday = DateTime.now().UnixTimestampMillis - 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000
local ok, value = pcall(function()
	return store:GetVersionAtTimeAsync("User_1", yesterday)
end)
print(ok, value)
kid.gotcha: The time must be above zero and not more than ten minutes in the future.

m.d:
This function returns a DataStoreKeyPages object for enumerating through keys of a data store. It accepts an optional prefix parameter to only locate keys whose names start with the provided prefix.

If DataStoreOptions.AllScopes was set to true when accessing the data store through DataStoreService:GetDataStore(), keys will be returned with all scopes as prefixes.
m.s: Returns a `Class.DataStoreKeyPages` object for enumerating through keys of a data store.

p.s: (Optional) Prefix to use for locating keys.
(Optional) Number of items to be returned in each page. If no value is given, the engine sends a default value of 0 to the data store web service, which in turn defaults to 50 items per page.
(Optional) Cursor to continue iteration.

(Optional) Exclude deleted keys from being returned.

When enabled ListKeys will check up to 512 keys. If all checked keys are deleted then it will return an empty list with a cursor to continue iteration.

r.s: A DataStoreKeyPages instance that enumerates the keys as DataStoreKey instances.

kid.simple: Lists the keys saved in this data store, page by page. Pass a prefix to only list keys that start with certain text.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")

local ok, pages = pcall(function()
	return store:ListKeysAsync("User_")
end)
if ok then
	for _, keyInfo in pages:GetCurrentPage() do
		print(keyInfo.KeyName)
	end
end

m.d: This function enumerates versions of the specified key in either ascending or descending order specified by a SortDirection parameter. It can optionally filter the returned versions by minimum and maximum timestamp.
m.s: Enumerates all versions of a key.

p.s: Key name for the versions to list. If DataStoreOptions.AllScopes was set to true when accessing the data store through DataStoreService:GetDataStore(), this key name must be prepended with the original scope as in "scope/key".
(Optional) Enum specifying ascending or descending sort order.
(Optional) Unix timestamp in milliseconds after which the versions should be listed.
(Optional) Unix timestamp in milliseconds up to which the versions should be listed.
(Optional) Number of items to be returned in each page. If no value is given, the engine sends a default value of 0 to the data store web service, which in turn defaults to 1024 items per page.

r.s: A DataStoreVersionPages instance that enumerates all the versions of the key as DataStoreObjectVersionInfo instances.

kid.simple: Lists all the saved versions of one key, oldest first or newest first. You can also limit it to a time range. Each item tells you the version id, when it was made, and whether it was a deletion.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")

local ok, pages = pcall(function()
	return store:ListVersionsAsync("User_1", Enum.SortDirection.Descending)
end)
if ok then
	for _, info in pages:GetCurrentPage() do
		print(info.Version, info.CreatedTime, info.IsDeleted)
	end
end

m.d:
This function permanently deletes the specified version of a key. Version identifiers can be found through DataStore:ListVersionsAsync().

Unlike GlobalDataStore:RemoveAsync(), this function does not create a new "tombstone" version and the removed value cannot be retrieved later.
m.s: Permanently deletes the specified version of a key.

p.s: Key name for which a version is to be removed. If DataStoreOptions.AllScopes was set to true when accessing the data store through DataStoreService:GetDataStore(), this key name must be prepended with the original scope as in "scope/key".
Version number of the key to remove.

m.dep: This method is deprecated. Do not use it for new work.

kid.simple: Old — do not use it in new work. Use RemoveAsync to delete a key; old versions expire on their own.

A DataStore is a named save box you get from `DataStoreService:GetDataStore`. It can do everything a GlobalDataStore can (Get, Set, Update, Increment, Remove), plus extra tools: it keeps older versions of each value, so you can look back in time, and it can list all its keys.
kid.analogy: A DataStore is like a notebook where every time you erase and rewrite a page, a photocopy of the old page is kept in a drawer for a while. You can look through the drawer to see what the page said yesterday.
whenToUse: Saving player data (this is the normal kind of data store to use).
Recovering a player's data from before a bug wiped it, using versions.
Admin tools that list all saved keys.

terms.data store: Roblox's save system. It keeps information (like coins or levels) even after players leave and servers shut down, and every server of your game shares it.
terms.key: The name you save a value under, like a label on a locker. A common key is `"User_" .. player.UserId`, for example `User_12345`.
terms.value: The thing stored under a key, like a number, text, true/false, or a table.
terms.server: The Roblox computer in charge of one copy of your game. Data stores can only be used from server Scripts.
terms.pcall: Short for 'protected call'. It runs a function and catches any error instead of letting your whole script crash. It gives back `true` plus the results if it worked, or `false` plus the error message if it failed.
terms.async / yield: Functions ending in `Async` talk to Roblox's computers over the internet, so they take a moment. While waiting, your script pauses (yields), then carries on when the answer arrives.
terms.rate limit / budget: How many data store requests a server is allowed to make per minute. For normal reads and writes the default is 60 + 40 for each player, so a server with 10 players can do 460 reads per minute. If you go over, requests are slowed down or dropped.
terms.UserId: A player's permanent ID number. It never changes, even if they change their name, so it makes a great key.
terms.version: A saved snapshot of a key's value. Each save makes a new version and older versions are kept for a while.
terms.Unix timestamp in milliseconds: A moment in time written as how many thousandths of a second have passed since January 1, 1970. `DateTime.now().UnixTimestampMillis` gives the current one.
terms.pages: Big lists come back split into pages, like a book. You read the current page, then ask for the next one.
terms.prefix: The beginning of a name. Listing with prefix `User_` only shows keys that start with `User_`.

examples.title: Save and load coins safely (pcall, retries, PlayerRemoving, BindToClose)
examples.code:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local coinStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")

-- Try a data store call up to 5 times, waiting longer each time
local function withRetries(callback)
	local waitTime = 1
	for attempt = 1, 5 do
		local ok, result = pcall(callback) -- catch errors instead of crashing
		if ok then
			return true, result
		end
		warn("Data store attempt " .. attempt .. " failed: " .. tostring(result))
		if attempt < 5 then
			task.wait(waitTime + math.random()) -- small random extra so servers don't all retry together
			waitTime *= 2 -- 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...
		end
	end
	return false, nil
end

local loaded = {} -- players whose data loaded safely

local function keyFor(player)
	return "User_" .. player.UserId
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	-- Make a leaderboard stat
	local leaderstats = Instance.new("Folder")
	leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
	local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
	coins.Name = "Coins"
	coins.Parent = leaderstats
	leaderstats.Parent = player

	-- Load saved coins
	local ok, saved = withRetries(function()
		return coinStore:GetAsync(keyFor(player))
	end)
	if ok then
		coins.Value = saved or 0 -- nil means a brand new player
		loaded[player] = true
	else
		warn("Could not load data for " .. player.Name .. ", will not save to protect it")
	end
end)

local function savePlayer(player)
	if not loaded[player] then
		return -- loading failed, so saving 0 would wipe their real coins
	end
	local leaderstats = player:FindFirstChild("leaderstats")
	local coins = leaderstats and leaderstats:FindFirstChild("Coins")
	if not coins then return end
	withRetries(function()
		return coinStore:SetAsync(keyFor(player), coins.Value, { player.UserId })
	end)
end

-- 1. Save when a player leaves
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
	savePlayer(player)
	loaded[player] = nil
end)

-- 2. Save everyone when the server shuts down
game:BindToClose(function()
	local stillSaving = 0
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		stillSaving += 1
		task.spawn(function() -- save all players at the same time
			savePlayer(player)
			stillSaving -= 1
		end)
	end
	-- Keep the server alive until every save finishes (Roblox allows up to 30 seconds)
	while stillSaving > 0 do
		task.wait()
	end
end)
explain: `GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")` opens a save box called PlayerCoins. Every server of your game sees the same box.
`withRetries` wraps each call in `pcall`. If Roblox's save servers have a hiccup, the script does not crash; it waits 1 second, then 2, then 4... and tries again, up to 5 times.
When a player joins, we load their coins with `GetAsync`. If nothing was saved yet we get nil, so we start at 0.
If loading failed every time, we remember NOT to save that player. Otherwise we would overwrite their real coins with 0.
`PlayerRemoving` saves the player's coins when they leave.

`game:BindToClose` runs when the server is shutting down (for example, the last player left or you updated the game). Without it, the server could close before saves finish. Roblox waits up to 30 seconds for this function.
Budgets: each server gets about 60 + 40 per player reads and writes per minute. One load per join and one save per leave stays far below that. Do NOT save every time a coin changes.

examples.title: Get a player's data from one hour ago
examples.code:
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")

local oneHourAgo = DateTime.now().UnixTimestampMillis - (60 * 60 * 1000)

local ok, oldValue = pcall(function()
	return store:GetVersionAtTimeAsync("User_12345", oneHourAgo)
end)
if ok then
	print("An hour ago the data was:", oldValue)
end
explain: We work out the time one hour ago in milliseconds (60 minutes x 60 seconds x 1000).
`GetVersionAtTimeAsync` returns the value that was saved at that moment, which can help undo a bad save.

gotchas: Data stores only work in server Scripts. A LocalScript cannot use them.

In Studio, data stores are off until you publish the game and turn on Game Settings > Security > Enable Studio Access to API Services. Studio uses the same data as the live game, so be careful, or use a separate test place.
Always wrap calls in `pcall`. They talk over the internet and can fail.
Never save in a fast loop or on every coin pickup. You will hit the rate limit. Save on leave, on shutdown, and maybe every few minutes as a backup.
If loading failed, do not save, or you may overwrite good data with empty data.
Keys must be 50 characters or fewer, and one key can hold up to about 4 MB. Text must be valid UTF-8.
Use `player.UserId` in keys, never the player's name (names can change).
You cannot save Instances like Parts or Color3/Vector3 values directly. Save numbers, strings, booleans and plain tables.
Listing keys and versions has a small budget (about 5 + 2 per player per minute). Do not use it during normal gameplay.

kid.simple: Gives you a normal data store by name, like opening a notebook called "PlayerCoins". If it does not exist yet, it is created the first time you save something. Calling it again with the same name gives the same data store.

-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local coinStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")

local ok, err = pcall(function()
	coinStore:SetAsync("User_1", 100)
end)
if not ok then warn(err) end

local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")

-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")

m.d:
Sets the per-server rate limit (requests per minute) for a given Data Store request type. The configured limit overrides the default rate limit for that request type on the current server. The rate limit is calculated as rateLimit = baseLimit + (perPlayerLimit * numPlayers), where numPlayers is the current number of active players on the server. DataStoreRequestType.OnUpdate and DataStoreRequestType.UpdateAsync cannot be configured with this function. Calling this API with those request types will result in an error.

You should call this API once per request type during server initialization. We don't recommend calling this API during active experience logic. If called multiple times, the new limit definitions will immediately overwrite the previous ones.

The baseLimit and perPlayerLimit have different constraints depending on the request type. See the table below for more information.

Request Type baseLimit constraints perPlayerLimit constraints

SetIncrementAsync [0, 60] [0, 40]

GetSortedAsync [0, 5] [0, 2]
SetIncrementSortedAsync [0, 30] [0, 5]
OnUpdate N/A N/A
ListAsync [0, 5] [0, 2]
GetVersionAsync [0, 5] [0, 2]
RemoveVersionAsync [0, 5] [0, 2]
StandardRead [0, 10000] [0, 200]
StandardWrite [0, 10000] [0, 200]
StandardList [0, 10000] [0, 200]
StandardRemove [0, 10000] [0, 200]
OrderedRead [0, 10000] [0, 200]
OrderedWrite [0, 10000] [0, 200]

kid.simple: Lets you choose how many requests of one kind this server may make per minute, using the formula: baseLimit + perPlayerLimit times the number of players. Call it once when the server starts if you want to use less of your game's shared budget.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService (run once at startup)
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")

-- 30 reads per minute, plus 20 more for each player
-- With 5 players: 30 + 20 * 5 = 130 reads per minute
DataStoreService:SetRateLimitForRequestType(Enum.DataStoreRequestType.StandardRead, 30, 20)
kid.gotcha: You cannot set limits for `UpdateAsync` or `OnUpdate` request types; that errors. Each type has allowed ranges for the two numbers.

kid.simple: DataStoreService is the doorway to Roblox's save system. It hands you data stores, which are like giant shared notebooks where your game can save things like coins, levels and inventories. Saved data stays even when players leave and servers close, and every server of your game can read it.
kid.analogy: DataStoreService is like the front desk of a huge locker room. You ask the desk for a locker room by name (a data store), then each player gets their own locker inside it, labeled with their ID number (a key).
whenToUse: Saving player progress (coins, level, items) so it is still there next time they play.
Making a global leaderboard of top scores (with an ordered data store).
Storing game-wide settings that every server should share.
kid.where: Server only. Get it with `game:GetService("DataStoreService")` in a Script in ServerScriptService.

terms.data store: Roblox's save system. It keeps information (like coins or levels) even after players leave and servers shut down, and every server of your game shares it.
terms.key: The name you save a value under, like a label on a locker. A common key is `"User_" .. player.UserId`, for example `User_12345`.
terms.value: The thing stored under a key, like a number, text, true/false, or a table.
terms.server: The Roblox computer in charge of one copy of your game. Data stores can only be used from server Scripts.
terms.client: A player's own device. LocalScripts on the client cannot use data stores at all.
terms.pcall: Short for 'protected call'. It runs a function and catches any error instead of letting your whole script crash. It gives back `true` plus the results if it worked, or `false` plus the error message if it failed.
terms.async / yield: Functions ending in `Async` talk to Roblox's computers over the internet, so they take a moment. While waiting, your script pauses (yields), then carries on when the answer arrives.
terms.retry: Trying again after a failure. Data store calls sometimes fail because of the internet, so good code waits a little and tries again a few times.
terms.rate limit / budget: How many data store requests a server is allowed to make per minute. For normal reads and writes the default is 60 + 40 for each player, so a server with 10 players can do 460 reads per minute. If you go over, requests are slowed down or dropped.
terms.throttle: When Roblox slows down or rejects your requests because you sent too many too fast.
terms.UserId: A player's permanent ID number. It never changes, even if they change their name, so it makes a great key.
terms.scope: An optional extra label that splits one data store into separate sections. Most games never need it; the default scope is `global`.
terms.BindToClose: `game:BindToClose(fn)` runs your function when the server is about to shut down, giving you up to 30 seconds to finish saving.
terms.PlayerRemoving: An event on the Players service that fires when a player is leaving. The usual moment to save their data.
terms.ordered data store: A special data store that only holds whole numbers and can sort them, perfect for leaderboards.
terms.Enum: A fixed list of named choices Roblox provides, like `Enum.DataStoreRequestType.StandardRead`.

examples.title: Save and load coins safely (pcall, retries, PlayerRemoving, BindToClose)
examples.code:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local coinStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")

-- Try a data store call up to 5 times, waiting longer each time
local function withRetries(callback)
	local waitTime = 1
	for attempt = 1, 5 do
		local ok, result = pcall(callback) -- catch errors instead of crashing
		if ok then
			return true, result
		end
		warn("Data store attempt " .. attempt .. " failed: " .. tostring(result))
		if attempt < 5 then
			task.wait(waitTime + math.random()) -- small random extra so servers don't all retry together
			waitTime *= 2 -- 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...
		end
	end
	return false, nil
end

local loaded = {} -- players whose data loaded safely

local function keyFor(player)
	return "User_" .. player.UserId
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	-- Make a leaderboard stat
	local leaderstats = Instance.new("Folder")
	leaderstats.Name = "leaderstats"
	local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
	coins.Name = "Coins"
	coins.Parent = leaderstats
	leaderstats.Parent = player

	-- Load saved coins
	local ok, saved = withRetries(function()
		return coinStore:GetAsync(keyFor(player))
	end)
	if ok then
		coins.Value = saved or 0 -- nil means a brand new player
		loaded[player] = true
	else
		warn("Could not load data for " .. player.Name .. ", will not save to protect it")
	end
end)

local function savePlayer(player)
	if not loaded[player] then
		return -- loading failed, so saving 0 would wipe their real coins
	end
	local leaderstats = player:FindFirstChild("leaderstats")
	local coins = leaderstats and leaderstats:FindFirstChild("Coins")
	if not coins then return end
	withRetries(function()
		return coinStore:SetAsync(keyFor(player), coins.Value, { player.UserId })
	end)
end

-- 1. Save when a player leaves
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
	savePlayer(player)
	loaded[player] = nil
end)

-- 2. Save everyone when the server shuts down

	local stillSaving = 0
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		stillSaving += 1
		task.spawn(function() -- save all players at the same time
			savePlayer(player)
			stillSaving -= 1
		end)
	end
	-- Keep the server alive until every save finishes (Roblox allows up to 30 seconds)
	while stillSaving > 0 do
		task.wait()
	end
end)
explain: `GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")` opens a save box called PlayerCoins. Every server of your game sees the same box.
`withRetries` wraps each call in `pcall`. If Roblox's save servers have a hiccup, the script does not crash; it waits 1 second, then 2, then 4... and tries again, up to 5 times.
When a player joins, we load their coins with `GetAsync`. If nothing was saved yet we get nil, so we start at 0.
If loading failed every time, we remember NOT to save that player. Otherwise we would overwrite their real coins with 0.
`PlayerRemoving` saves the player's coins when they leave.

`game:BindToClose` runs when the server is shutting down (for example, the last player left or you updated the game). Without it, the server could close before saves finish. Roblox waits up to 30 seconds for this function.
Budgets: each server gets about 60 + 40 per player reads and writes per minute. One load per join and one save per leave stays far below that. Do NOT save every time a coin changes.

examples.title: Check your request budget before a big job
examples.code:
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")

local function waitForBudget(requestType)
	-- Pause until we are allowed at least one more request
	while DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType(requestType) < 1 do
		task.wait(1)
	end
end

local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("Settings")
waitForBudget(Enum.DataStoreRequestType.StandardRead)
local ok, value = pcall(function()
	return store:GetAsync("EventName")
end)
print(ok, value)
explain: The budget is how many requests of a type this server can still make right now.
If it is 0, we wait a second and check again instead of getting throttled.

gotchas: Data stores only work in server Scripts. A LocalScript cannot use them.

In Studio, data stores are off until you publish the game and turn on Game Settings > Security > Enable Studio Access to API Services. Studio uses the same data as the live game, so be careful, or use a separate test place.
Always wrap calls in `pcall`. They talk over the internet and can fail.
Never save in a fast loop or on every coin pickup. You will hit the rate limit. Save on leave, on shutdown, and maybe every few minutes as a backup.
If loading failed, do not save, or you may overwrite good data with empty data.
Keys must be 50 characters or fewer, and one key can hold up to about 4 MB. Text must be valid UTF-8.
Use `player.UserId` in keys, never the player's name (names can change).
You cannot save Instances like Parts or Color3/Vector3 values directly. Save numbers, strings, booleans and plain tables.

class/Debris.d:
The Debris service allows scheduling guaranteed destruction of an object without yielding.

Advantages

Besides creating a bit of a mess, objects that are no longer required can use up system memory and cause an experience to run slower over time. For this reason, it's always advised to call Instance:Destroy() on objects you no longer need. In some cases, however, an object may have a specific period of utility before it can be destroyed.

Consider a wall being smashed into individual bricks. If you want a brick to linger for 3 seconds before being destroyed, you can use the following code:

task.wait(3)
brick:Destroy()

However, waiting causes the thread to yield which may be undesired. To avoid yielding, a callback function can be scheduled to run on a new thread after 3 seconds:

task.delay(3, function()
    brick:Destroy()
end)

Or in one line:

task.delay(3, brick.Destroy, brick)

While this now avoids yielding, it has a potential drawback in that the scheduled callback will never run if the script is disabled or destroyed before the callback runs.

This is where Debris has a specific advantage, as it does not yield the current thread and runs outside the context of the script, guaranteeing the instance is eventually destroyed even if the script is disabled or destroyed. The following code does not yield and guarantees the instance will be destroyed:

Debris:AddItem(brick, 3)

Note that Debris has a hardcoded maximum of 1,000 objects, so if more than 1,000 items are added, the oldest debris will be destroyed instantly to make room for new debris.
class/Debris.s: Allows scheduling the guaranteed destruction of an object without yielding.

m.d:
The maximum number of items that can be assigned to the Debris service at one time.

If this number is exceeded, objects are automatically destroyed in order from oldest to newest until the amount is less than or equal to MaxItems.

This property is currently restricted and will error if set. The value is hardcoded to 1,000 items.
m.s: The maximum number of items that can be assigned to the `Class.Debris` service at one time.

kid.simple: Old — it is ignored now. Debris always holds up to 1,000 items.

m.d:
Schedules a given Instance for destruction within the specified lifetime. After the lifetime argument has elapsed, the object is destroyed in the same manner as Instance:Destroy(). Note that the lifetime argument is optional and defaults to 10 seconds.

Note that Debris has a hardcoded maximum of 1,000 objects, so if more than 1,000 items are added, the oldest debris will be destroyed instantly to make room for new debris. This means you should treat the lifetime parameter as a maximum lifetime, not an exact lifetime.
m.s: Schedules a given `Class.Instance` for destruction within the specified lifetime.

p.s: The Instance to add to Debris.
Number of seconds before the Instance should be destroyed.

kid.simple: Schedules an object to be destroyed after a number of seconds (10 if you leave it out). It does not pause your script.
kid.example:
local Debris = game:GetService("Debris")

local spark = Instance.new("Part")
spark.Anchored = true
spark.Parent = workspace
Debris:AddItem(spark, 2) -- gone in 2 seconds
kid.gotcha: If more than 1,000 objects are waiting, the oldest are removed early.

m.dep: This function is a deprecated variant of Debris:AddItem() which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `Debris:AddItem` instead (with a capital A).

Debris is a cleanup crew. You give it an object and a number of seconds, and when the time is up it destroys that object for you. Your script does not have to stop and wait, and the cleanup still happens even if your script is turned off or deleted.
kid.analogy: Debris is like putting a note on an item saying "throw this away in 5 seconds" and handing it to the janitor. You can walk away and keep working; the janitor will take care of it no matter what.
whenToUse: Remove bullets, sparks, broken bricks or effects after a few seconds
Clean up a temporary object without pausing your script
Make sure something gets removed even if the script that made it is destroyed
kid.where: Server and client. Get it with game:GetService("Debris").

terms.destroy: To delete an object from the game for good, the same as calling `:Destroy()` on it.
terms.lifetime: How many seconds the object is allowed to stay before Debris removes it.
terms.yield: To pause your script. Debris does not yield, so your code keeps going right away.
terms.memory: The space your game uses to remember things. Lots of leftover objects use more memory and can make the game slower.

examples.title: Drop a brick that disappears after 3 seconds
examples.code:
local Debris = game:GetService("Debris")

for i = 1, 5 do
    local brick = Instance.new("Part")
    brick.Size = Vector3.new(1, 1, 1)
    brick.Position = Vector3.new(i * 2, 20, 0)
    brick.Parent = workspace

    Debris:AddItem(brick, 3) -- remove this brick in 3 seconds

    task.wait(0.5) -- one brick every half second
end
print("All bricks dropped")
explain: We create 5 bricks high up so they fall.
`Debris:AddItem(brick, 3)` schedules each brick to be destroyed 3 seconds later.
AddItem does not pause, so the loop keeps going and drops the next brick.

gotchas: Debris can only hold 1,000 objects at once. If you add more, the oldest ones are destroyed right away. So think of the time as the MOST it will stay, not an exact time.
If you leave out the seconds, the default is 10 seconds.
Do not use the object after it is destroyed. Check that it still has a Parent first.
`task.delay(3, function() brick:Destroy() end)` also works, but stops if the script is destroyed; Debris keeps working anyway.

class/Decal.d:
The Decal object applies an image texture to a face of a parent BasePart. The affected face is dependent on the Face property, and the size of the decal is dependent on the size of the face.

The applied image texture is determined by its ColorMapContent property. For details on how to upload images, see asset management.

For more information, review textures and decals. See also:

  • Texture for repeating surface images.
  • MeshPart.TextureContent to apply an image texture to a MeshPart.
  • SurfaceGui to apply an ImageLabel or ImageButton to an in-experience 3D object.
class/Decal.s: Applies an image texture to a face of a parent `Class.BasePart`.

m.d:
When set to true, the decal's image asset is eligible for automatic localization through the Automatic Asset Capture system. The LocalizationService uses this property to determine whether the decal's ColorMapContent should be captured and potentially replaced with a localized version.

This property only applies to non-PBR decals. If any PBR maps (NormalMapContent, RoughnessMapContent, MetalnessMapContent, or EmissiveMaskContent) are set, automatic localization capture is suppressed to avoid inconsistent rendering.
m.s: When set to `true`, the decal's image asset is eligible for automatic localization capture.

m.d: The Color3 tint of the Decal. Note that this property only sets the tint of the decal rather than the color; unless the image associated with the Decal was originally pure white, then the color cannot be freely changed using this property.
m.s: The `Datatype.Color3` tint of the `Class.Decal`.

m.d: This property takes a content ID to determine the color and opacity of the surface. This texture is sometimes called the albedo texture.
m.s: Content ID that determines the color and opacity of the surface.

m.d: This property takes a Content object to determine the color and opacity of the surface. This texture is sometimes called the albedo texture.
m.s: `Datatype.Content` object that determines the color and opacity of the surface.

m.d:
This property takes a Content object that determines the apparent emissivity across the surface. An emissive mask is a grayscale image where black pixels correspond to no emissivity and white pixels correspond to full emissivity. It defaults to an empty content, in which case the decal doesn't glow.

The emissive contribution is added to the total lighting contribution across the surface, and the sum is multiplied by the albedo texture from ColorMapContent, if provided. Use EmissiveStrength and EmissiveTint to control how bright the glow is and what color it has.

Assigning an emissive mask makes the Decal a physically based rendering (PBR) surface.
m.s: `Datatype.Content` object that determines the emissivity across the surface.

m.d:
This value is a multiplier that controls how strong the emissive contribution from EmissiveMaskContent is across the surface. Defaults to 1. Negative values are treated as 0, and a value of 0 turns off the glow.

If the final emissive contribution goes beyond the supported dynamic range, it's clamped, which can make the emissive areas appear fully white at large strength values. Since this value is a multiplier, the maximum value that avoids clamping depends on the other contributing values, including EmissiveTint, ColorMapContent, and the combined lighting contribution.
m.s: Determines the strength of the emissive contribution.

m.d: This value is a Color3 that tints the emissive contribution from EmissiveMaskContent. Defaults to white, which leaves the emissive color unchanged. Each component is clamped between 0 and 1, and black turns off the glow.
m.s: Determines the tinting color for the emissive contribution.

m.d:
Acts as a multiplier for the decal's Transparency property. The effect is only visible to the LocalPlayer and will not replicate to the server.

When this property is set to 1, the Decal will be completely invisible regardless of its original transparency. When it is set to 0, the decal's rendered transparency will match the Transparency value.
m.s: Acts as a multiplier for the decal's `Class.Decal.Transparency|Transparency` property. The effects are only visible to the local player.

m.d:
This property takes a content ID that determines the metalness map applied to the surface. A metalness map controls how metallic the surface appears at each point, blending between a dielectric (non-metal) and a metallic response to light. It defaults to an empty content, in which case no metalness map is applied.

Assigning a normal, roughness, metalness, or emissive map makes the Decal a physically based rendering (PBR) surface. To assign this map from a Content object, use MetalnessMapContent.
m.s: Content ID that determines the metalness map of the surface.

m.d:

Determines the transparency of the Decal with 0 being completely opaque and 1 completely transparent.

class/Dialog.d: The Dialog object allows users to create non-player characters (NPCs) that players can talk to using a list of choices. The Dialog object can be inserted into a part such as a Humanoid's head, and then a player will see a speech bubble above the part that they can click on to start a conversation. The creator of a place can choose what choices the player can say by inserting DialogChoice objects into the dialog.

m.d:
The BehaviorType of a Dialog determines whether multiple players can interact with a dialog at once. The default value for this property is SinglePlayer.

SinglePlayer

When a Dialog is configured to SinglePlayer, only one player can interact with it at a time. As soon as a player engages with a dialog, other players will not be able to initiate the dialog until the first player is finished.

While a player is engaged with a dialog, the other players will see the dialog choices of the player who started the dialog, along with the responses.

MultiplePlayers

When a Dialog is set to MultiplePlayers, any player can initiate a dialog at any time, even if another player has already initiated the dialog. Unlike SinglePlayer however, Dialogs set to MultiplePlayers will not show the dialog choices and responses to anyone but the player in the conversation.
m.s: Sets whether the Dialog can be used by multiple players at once.

m.d:
The maximum distance in studs between the player's character and the Dialog's parent BasePart at which the player can click on the speech bubble to begin or continue a conversation. If the player moves further than this distance from the parent part, they cannot initiate the dialog. The engine uses this value to select the nearest available Dialog when multiple are in range.

Default is 25.
m.s: The furthest distance that a player can be from the Dialog's parent to start a conversation.

m.d: Toggles whether the goodbye option will be displayed. If true, the dialog will display the content of Dialog.GoodbyeDialog as the last option after other dialog choices. Clicking on the goodbye option will exit the dialog.
m.s: Toggles whether the goodbye option will be displayed.

m.d:
The text displayed as the goodbye option at the bottom of the dialog choices list. When Dialog.GoodbyeChoiceActive is true, this string appears as the final selectable choice; clicking it ends the conversation. When Dialog.GoodbyeChoiceActive is false, this property has no visible effect.

Default is an empty string.
m.s: Sets the sentence that the dialog will show to the player when the chat ends.

m.d:
The text that the NPC displays inside the speech bubble when a player first begins the conversation. This is the opening line that appears before the player selects from DialogChoice options nested under this Dialog.

Default is an empty string.
m.s: Sets the first sentence that the dialog will show to the player, once a chat is commenced.

m.d:
A read-only runtime indicator that is true whenever at least one player is currently engaged in this dialog conversation. The engine sets this to true when a player begins talking and resets it to false when all participants leave. This property is not serialized and always starts as false when the place loads. Scripts can read this property but cannot set it directly.

Default is false.
m.s: If true, this dialog is being used by at least one player.

Default is Help.

Default is 0, which effectively disables the distance-based trigger indicator; the player must be within Dialog.ConversationDistance to see and interact with the dialog.

class/DraftsService.d:
DraftsService backs the collaborative editing "drafts" workflow in a Team Create session. When collaborative editing is enabled, a collaborator's changes to a Script, LocalScript, or ModuleScript are kept as a local draft rather than being applied to the shared session copy immediately, and a draft must be committed before other collaborators receive it.

The service exposes the operations behind Studio's Drafts interface. GetDrafts() enumerates the current drafts, GetDraftStatus() reports a draft's status, and GetEditors() lists the collaborators editing a given script. CommitEdits() and DiscardEdits() publish or drop changes; RestoreScripts() and UpdateToLatestVersion() reconcile local drafts with the server; and ShowDiffsAgainstBase() and ShowDiffsAgainstServer() open diff views. Events including DraftAdded, DraftRemoved, DraftStatusChanged, and EditorsListChanged fire as drafts and their editors change.

DraftsService is a Studio-only service; retrieve it with game:GetService("DraftsService").
class/DraftsService.s: A Studio service that manages script drafts in a Team Create session with collaborative editing enabled.

class/DragDetector.d:
The DragDetector instance facilitates and encourages interaction with 3D objects in an experience, such as opening doors and drawers, sliding a part around, and much more. Key features include:

  • Place a DragDetector under any BasePart or Model to make it draggable via all inputs (mouse, touch, gamepad, and VR), all without a single line of code.

  • Choose from several DragStyle options, define how the object responds to motion via ResponseStyle, and optionally apply axis or movement limits.

  • Scripts can respond to manipulation of dragged objects to drive UI or make logical decisions, such as adjusting the light level in a room based on a sliding wall switch dimmer.

  • Players can manipulate anchored parts or models and they'll stay exactly where you put them upon release.

  • DragDetectors work in Studio as long as you're not using the Select, Move, Scale, or Rotate tools, making it easier to test and adjust draggable objects while editing.

See the 3D Drag Detectors guide for details and usage examples.

The Dragger object is a helper object used to create tools that can drag parts. It is expected (but not required) to be used with Mouse events.

Primarily used with the RbxStamper library.
class/Dragger.s: A helper object used to create tools that can drag parts.
class/Dragger.dep: This class has been deprecated, as it does not work well with FilteringEnabled, and should not be used in new work.

m.d:
Rotates the currently dragged part(s) by 90 degrees around the specified world axis. This method can only be called while a drag is actively in progress (after Dragger:MouseDown() has been called and Dragger:MouseMove() has initiated movement). The axis parameter defaults to Axis.X.

For single-part drags the rotation is performed about the snap face axis. For multi-part drags the rotation is applied around the computed center of the part group using a collision-aware routine that prevents overlap with surrounding geometry.
m.s: Rotates the currently dragged part(s) by 90 degrees on the given axis.

p.s: The Axis (X, Y, or Z) around which to rotate.

m.d:
Initializes a dragging action by registering the parts to drag and the point on the mouse part where the interaction began. This method does not immediately begin moving parts; actual movement starts on a subsequent Dragger:MouseMove() call once the mouse has moved beyond a break-free threshold (half the current grid snap distance).

mousePart must be a BasePart that is both a member of parts and a descendant of Workspace. Calling this method while a drag is already active (before Dragger:MouseUp()) throws an error. While a drag is pending, camera mouse-pan is disabled so that mouse movement applies to the drag instead of the viewport.
m.s: Initializes a dragging action, specifying which parts to use when dragging.

p.s: The BasePart under the mouse that serves as the drag handle. Must be a member of parts and must be in the Workspace.
A Vector3 in the local coordinate space of mousePart indicating where the mouse initially contacted the part.
An array of BaseParts to move together during the drag. Must include mousePart and contain at least one element.

m.d:
Attempts to move the currently dragged parts to the location indicated by mouseRay. Must be called after Dragger:MouseDown().

On the first call that detects sufficient mouse movement (exceeding half the grid snap distance), the method transitions into active dragging: it un-joins the dragged parts from surrounding geometry, aligns them to the grid, and begins tracking movement. On each subsequent call, the ray is cast against other parts in the Workspace (or against the world ground plane at Y = 0 if nothing is hit), and the dragged parts are moved toward that snap point using a collision-aware algorithm that prevents them from overlapping existing geometry. Single-part drags use surface snapping; multi-part drags use grid-aligned displacement with Y-drop collision avoidance.
m.s: Tries to move the currently dragged part to the point where MouseRay hits another part.

p.s: A Ray representing the current mouse position in world space (origin at the camera, direction toward the pointer).

m.d:
Stops the current dragging action initiated by Dragger:MouseDown(). If parts were actively being dragged, this method re-joins them to adjacent geometry and finalizes their position. If MouseDown was called but the mouse never moved far enough to begin actual dragging, the state is simply reset. In both cases camera mouse-pan is re-enabled.

Calling this method without a prior Dragger:MouseDown() throws an error.
m.s: Stops the current dragging action (made by `Class.Dragger:MouseDown()`).

class/DraggerService.d: DraggerService is a central hub for dragger-related settings that Studio's dragging tools (and other dragger-like editing UX) read when deciding how to move, snap, and highlight objects. Because the Move, Scale, and Rotate tools all consult the same service, changing a setting here keeps their snapping, collision, joint, and hover behavior in sync. Each property reflects the corresponding Studio editing preference or global editing state.
class/DraggerService.s: A service that centralizes the global dragger settings that Studio's dragging tools read so they move, snap, and highlight objects consistently.

m.d: When true, a dragged object is rotated to align with the surface it is dropped on instead of keeping its original orientation. This reflects Studio's "Align Dragged Objects" editing preference and is read by the dragging tools.
m.s: Whether a dragged object is re-aligned to the surface it is dropped onto.

m.d: When true, rotating an object with a dragger snaps the rotation to multiples of DraggerService.AngleSnapIncrement. When false, rotation is continuous and the increment has no effect.
m.s: Whether rotation drags snap to multiples of `Class.DraggerService.AngleSnapIncrement`.

m.d: The rotation snapping step, in degrees, applied while DraggerService.AngleSnapEnabled is true; it has no effect when angle snapping is disabled. The value is clamped to a small positive minimum, so it can never be set to 0 or a negative number.
m.s: The angle, in degrees, that rotation drags snap to.

m.d: When true, the highlight drawn over the object under the cursor animates (pulses) at DraggerService.HoverAnimateFrequency. It only has a visible effect when DraggerService.ShowHover is true.
m.s: Whether the hover highlight pulses instead of staying static.

m.d: When true, dragging performs collision checking so that a moved object stops against other parts instead of passing through them. When false, objects can be dragged freely through existing geometry.
m.s: Whether draggers prevent a moved object from overlapping other geometry.

m.d: Controls the coordinate space draggers operate in: DraggerCoordinateSpace.Object moves and rotates relative to the object's own orientation, while DraggerCoordinateSpace.World uses the global axes. Defaults to DraggerCoordinateSpace.Object.
m.s: Whether drag transforms are applied in the object's local space or in world space.

m.d: Selects how draggers compute movement: DraggerMovementMode.Geometric applies transforms directly, while DraggerMovementMode.Physical respects physical constraints while dragging. Defaults to DraggerMovementMode.Geometric.
m.s: Whether dragging moves objects geometrically or by respecting physical constraints.

m.d: The Color3 used to draw the snapping indicators (such as pivot-to-geometry snap points) shown while dragging. It reflects the corresponding Studio color preference.
m.s: The color of the on-screen indicators drawn when a drag snaps to geometry.

m.d: How fast the hover highlight pulses, in cycles per second, when DraggerService.AnimateHover is true. The value corresponds to Studio's hover-animation speed preference, which ranges from 0.5 (very slow) to 10 (very fast).
m.s: The frequency, in hertz, at which the hover highlight animates.

m.d: The thickness of the outline drawn around the object beneath the cursor. It is only visible when DraggerService.ShowHover is true, and reflects Studio's hover-outline thickness preference.
m.s: The thickness of the highlight outline drawn around the object under the cursor.

m.d: When true, parts that come to rest against other surfaces during a drag are joined to them (for example, surface welds) when the drag finishes. When false, dragging does not create joints.
m.s: Whether draggers create surface joints between touching parts when a drag ends.

m.d: When true, moving an object with a dragger snaps its position to a grid whose spacing is DraggerService.LinearSnapIncrement. When false, movement is continuous and the increment has no effect.
m.s: Whether positional drags snap to a grid of `Class.DraggerService.LinearSnapIncrement`.

m.d: The spacing, in studs, of the movement grid applied while DraggerService.LinearSnapEnabled is true; it has no effect when linear snapping is disabled. The value is clamped to a small positive minimum, so it can never be set to 0 or a negative number.
m.s: The grid size, in studs, that positional drags snap to.

m.d: When true, dragging snaps the moved object to salient points (such as edges and corners) on nearby parts, in addition to any grid snapping. When false, part-to-part snapping is off.
m.s: Whether draggers snap to alignment points on nearby parts.

m.d: When true, dragging an object's pivot snaps it to points on surrounding geometry (for example vertices, edges, and face centers). When false, the pivot moves freely.
m.s: Whether an object's pivot snaps to points on nearby geometry while it is being edited.

m.d: When true, draggers draw a highlight over the object beneath the cursor to indicate what a drag would affect. When false, no hover highlight is shown and DraggerService.AnimateHover, DraggerService.HoverThickness, and DraggerService.HoverAnimateFrequency have no visible effect.
m.s: Whether a highlight is drawn over the object currently under the cursor.

m.d: When true, the pivot indicator (the marker showing an object's pivot point) is shown while dragging. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether to show the pivot indicator for a selected object as it's being dragged.

m.d: When true, the dragging tools use the axis-aligned bounding box of an object for snapping instead of its precise geometric shape. This can simplify placement when objects have complex geometry. The setting corresponds to Studio's "Use Bounding Boxes" option in the dragger-settings ribbon dropdown. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether draggers use axis-aligned bounding boxes rather than precise geometry for snapping calculations.
